key_concepts: reflection at tissue boundaries due to acoustic impedance change
time delay gives depth of boundary
reflected intensity gives nature of boundary
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about how the ultrasound gets into the body in the first place - what device makes a short burst of high-frequency sound and also listens for what comes back?
Hint 2: Think about what happens when a sound wave travelling through one type of tissue meets a different type of tissue - why would some of it come back?
Hint 3: If you measure how long it takes for the echo to return, what does that time tell you about how far inside the body the reflection happened?
Hint 4: If one echo comes back very strong and another comes back very weak, what does the strength tell you about the boundary it reflected from?
Hint 5: Pull the story together - how do many pulses in different directions, plus good contact with the skin, build up a full diagnostic image?
parts.proper_answer: A transducer emits a short pulse of ultrasound into the body. A coupling medium (gel) ensures good transmission. At a boundary between tissues the pulse is partly reflected and partly transmitted. The reflected pulse is detected by the transducer. The time delay between emission and detection gives the depth of the boundary. The intensity of the reflected pulse gives information about the nature of the tissues at the boundary. Processing of many pulses builds an image of internal structures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Send In a Short Pulse**
Think of ultrasound imaging like sonar inside the body. A piezoelectric transducer acts as both loudspeaker and microphone. It sends out a very short burst of ultrasound, typically in the MHz range, into the body. A layer of gel is used on the skin to remove air and allow maximum transmission of the ultrasound into the tissue.

Step 2: **Reflection at Internal Boundaries**
As the pulse travels, it meets boundaries between different tissues, for example muscle and bone or fluid and soft tissue. Each tissue has a different acoustic impedance $Z$. Where $Z$ changes, part of the wave energy is reflected back toward the surface and part continues deeper. This is the key physics - no reflection without a change in properties.

Step 3: **Time Delay Tells You Depth**
The same transducer now detects the returning echo. If the speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is $c$ and the measured time between sending and receiving is $t$, the wave has travelled there and back, so the depth $d$ is given by $$d = \frac{c t}{2}$$ A longer delay means a deeper structure. This is how distance is measured.

Step 4: **Intensity Tells You Nature**
Not all echoes are equal. A large difference in acoustic impedance gives a strong, high-intensity reflection, while a small difference gives a weak reflection. So the amplitude of the detected signal tells you about the nature of the boundary and the type of tissues involved.

Step 5: **Build the Diagnostic Image**
By sending pulses in many directions and recording both the time and strength of each echo, a processor builds up a 2D image of the positions and types of internal structures. That is why ultrasound can show the size, shape and position of organs, a fetus, or abnormal growths safely and non-invasively.
